Now that the demonstration of the possibility of our new invention has been shown briefly, and no less sufficiently, I do not think that I myself should be wearied any longer on this same occasion, since the route and method extends to infinity, if anyone should need an example for further matters. Nor do I think it at all necessary to recall to memory the things that have been recited in the preceding sections, since the keen reader, if he is studious, will also be able, with the Lord’s help, to discover the greater things that lie hidden in these matters. We have handed over to the wise and studious man both the material and the cause; if he wishes to use them prudently, he will surpass us by his own talent. But whoever desires this path to be more beautiful in the shade, let him join hand and mind to talent, and let him make for himself a route more beautifully adorned by paraphrase. If these things delight anyone, let him keep it fixed in memory that he must always remain within the prescribed circle; if he passes beyond it in any way, the whole operation vanishes uselessly. There are many names of men; indeed there are almost infinite words for things, villages, cities, provinces, trees, stones, and words, all of which serve our purposes. From these it is clear that a book and a method can be made, not impossibly, if talent is present together with diligence, which may surpass our inventions infinitely. But he who is of such dullness that he cannot understand these childish things of ours, when will he penetrate the subtler things that remain? We set an end to the fourth book of the Polygraphy, to which we join the fifth, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

End of the Fourth Book of the Polygraphy

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James the Apostle at Wurzburg. The Fifth Book of the Polygraphia: the beginning

Those things which, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have set forth, in whatever manner, in the four preceding books for the completion of our Polygraphia, reasonably require that we briefly treat, in the fifth, the remaining precepts and methods of this instruction which are left. Therefore in it we shall give a sufficiently concise method by metathesis, that is, by transposition of letters, by which a friend may write to a friend securely, safely, and most secretly whatever he wishes. We read that Caesar Augustus used this mode of writing in secret matters. And although this method of communication is secure in many ways, nevertheless it is always regarded with suspicion by those who look at it: for as soon as a transposition of letters is perceived, anyone curious at once suspects that something lies hidden beneath them. Now the methods of this invention are almost infinite; from them, for the necessary introduction, we have marked out the following for the reader, leaving the rest to be investigated by his own ingenuity. First, therefore, we have placed before him the canonical table of this craft, to which we have added beneath another, reversed one. In these two tables the root and foundation of the aforesaid transposition is wholly set down, upon which the structure of the whole edifice is placed. For when these two tables have been duly known and understood, no transposition of letters will be able to remain hidden from one working carefully. To these we have joined twenty-four alphabets in order, so that we might furnish the reader with an abundance for transposing letters. The use of these, according to one’s wish, consists in each single one, or, if you prefer, even in all of them. If you have secret dealings with many people, assign the individual alphabets to your individual intimates, and commit to memory what you have handed over to each.

Hand over the first alphabet to the first man, the second to the second, the third to the third, and so let it be done in sequence with the rest. But if, because of the multitude of affairs or of one’s household, the alphabets which we have marked out should not suffice for everything, or if some of them seem too open and plain, we shall be able to introduce various new transpositions, of which both the number is very great and the method of the secret may always remain perpetually hidden. Let us set down an example of this matter: let B be a, f be b, l be c, p be d, t be e, z be f, c be g, m be h, and so consequently let it be done through the whole usual alphabet, so that between any assumed letter three idle and transposed letters may intervene. Afterwards four, then five, more or fewer, yet in such a way that the whole alphabet, as though turned around in a circle, comes together, and no letter at all is omitted, but each is placed for another in its own order in the same series. In whatever way you have written it, it must be committed firmly to memory, lest, having fallen into forgetfulness, you yourself can no longer read what you had written. For the transposition of letters can be varied in as many ways as, according to the estimation of the human intellect, which, enclosed in a mortal body by temporal operation, does not properly grasp infinities, an innumerable mortal number will arise. Hence anyone who wishes to have more methods of writing by metathesis, and ones removed from our instruction, if he is even a little ingenious and diligent, will obtain an easy result in his work. For the human intellect can do very great things if it is aided by study and art. But he who despises the smallest things will never attain to greater ones. I know that there will be very many who will deride these studies of ours as empty and childish; to them we give as a reply that we shall be wholly content, provided they please those at whose insistence they have been composed by us.

Prima figura expansionis tabulae rectae:

Original linear rendering

The Straight Table of Transposition

[A transposition grid of the 24-letter alphabet (a b d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t u x y z w), each successive row shifted by one — rendered as printed.]

In this canonical or straight table of letters you have, from our one and usual [alphabet] of Latin letters themselves, by their permutation or transposition, as many alphabets as there are monograms throughout it—namely four-and-twenty times twenty-four, which make in number 576; and multiplied by as many again, they yield a little less than fourteen thousand.

[d ij]

The Reverse Table of Transposition

[A reverse transposition grid, as printed.]

In this reverse table you have, by the transposition of letters, as many alphabets as we likewise marked out in the preceding straight [table]. For, as you see, under the metathesis there are 24 to the right; to the left likewise as many; downward 24. Which, multiplied 24 times by 98, reduced in the form of a cross to the four sides, make alphabets not fewer than 112.

There follows the same table expanded.

ORCHEMA.

|a|b|c|d|e|f|g|h|i|k|l|m|n|o|p|r|q;s;t;u;x;y;z; |A|B|C|D|E|F|G|H|I|K|L|M|N|O|P|R|Q;S;T;U;X;Y;Z;

In the present orchema a multiple alphabet is handed down through transposition and leap, both by the rule of order and by the position of the letters. All these things suffice as an example for those who cannot be content with the things set in place, so that they may have a method and form for discovering the things that remain, because they can be varied without number.

Quinta figura expansionis tabulae rectae.

Original linear rendering

Johannes Trithemius, [unclear] abbot, greets the reader.

Since the letters of the Greeks and the Hebrews are all numerical, I have often wondered that the careful Latin usage of the ancients did not also make its own letters serve in the reckoning of numbers. The Hebrews, by duplicating certain letters, established twenty-eight signs, sufficient for every number. The Greeks, with like foresight, remedied this deficiency of letters by adding four characters. Since we therefore have twenty-four letters, why do we not make ours numerical too, we who can similarly find four duplicated letters? Let us give four as an example, and there will be enough for every number: [unclear] and final [j?]; likewise long s and final or closed s; likewise closed v and open u. When we add these to the twenty-three usual letters, we have twenty-eight characters sufficient for all numbers. And it will be no great labor to grasp this method of numbering for those who already know the letters, if they once commit it to memory. For this invention of ours will be able to be useful to many, since in a few letters it comprises many thousands in number, all of which can be discerned and understood at first sight, more clearly than light, without any calculation. Many who are less experienced in the art of calculation think that this cannot be done so easily by the figures of algorism, especially in large numbers. For as soon as you have looked with your eye upon a number, however large, you will be able both to understand it fully and to express it without circumlocution or division of speech. Since this is so easy, it is fitting that we set down the letters themselves reduced to number. I wrote this on 16 March in the year 1508.

Behold, reader, you have the method by which you can adequately set down and write every writable number in a few letters, whose extension, as you see, proceeds to infinity. But as it was once customary to say in a proverb, the tired ox plants his foot firmly: whoever wishes to be content with the former things should follow the old method of numbering. So that those who do not know it may understand it more easily, it will not be tedious for me to give in what follows the form which Hunibald, historiographer of the Franks, and also Bede, Rabanus, Helperic, monks, and several of the ancients used in chronicles and ecclesiastical calculations, as follows.

We have set forth up to this point, by way of example, the ancient manner of the Germans and Franks of writing numbers with Latin letters, so that we might also furnish knowledge of it to those who do not know it. But as for the fact that, in the placement of the figures of algorism, we have departed from the common rule of computation, this was done not from error but for a reasonable cause, namely so that we should not be overburdened in an excessive progression. There were also some who wrote larger numbers in this manner.

Secunda figura expansionis tabulae rectae.

Original linear rendering

Before all invention and use of letters, in the beginning of the world, when human beings were still crude in understanding and uncultivated in manners, under the [unclear] governance of alternation, as some suppose, of the intelligences, succeeding one another in order for one thousand sixty-three years, they were, in the sphere of the planets, by their influence exercising power in their own fashion over bodies on earth. The ancient speculators on this matter say that Saturn, from the beginning of the world, presided by his influence over things germinating and springing up on the earth, principally through his governing intelligence, which they called Orisiel, that is, “the vivifier of God,” for three hundred fifty-four lunar years, likewise four months, and the same number of days and hours. We recount these things as poetic fictions; we do not affirm them. After Saturn, Venus; after Venus, Jupiter is said to have assumed dominion. But after Jupiter, Mercury, fourth ruler in order, adorned the talents of human beings with various arts. Under the three intelligences just mentioned, namely while Saturn, Venus, and Jupiter were ruling, they report that human beings did not have the use or knowledge of letters. Hence whenever one person wished to announce some secret matter to another, he did this not by writings, since the service of letters was lacking, but symbolically, by certain likenesses of animals, trees and plants, or of some other perceptible things, according as each had agreed among themselves. The time of Saturn, they say, gave to human beings manners properly corresponding to his influence. For it made them farmers, hunters, founders of cities, crude, woodland-dwelling, gloomy, simple, uncultivated in life and manners, and living for a long time in the flesh. After Orisiel of Saturn, as those who hold such opinions say, the intelligence Anael, mover of Venus, receiving the governance of the world by influence, continued it for three hundred fifty-four years, months, days, and four hours. Under him human beings began to be more cultivated, to construct houses more frequently and cities, and also to invent various manual arts, namely the work of weaving, wool-working, and many other things similar to these. They also began to flow more fully into the pleasures of the flesh, and to take beautiful wives; and with many children begotten from them, they notably fell away from natural simplicity. They invented games and songs, began to play the cithara, and whatever they affirm to pertain to the influence of Venus they devised more zealously, following the impulse of the flesh too much. They named the third intelligence, that of Jupiter, Zachariel; and when it took up dominion of the world after Anael, it made human beings restless with desire to rule, to go hunting, to make tents, and to adorn themselves with various garments. While he ruled, in accordance with the quality of Jupiter, who deprived his father of the kingdom, there arose a great division between the good and the bad, the former calling upon God, the latter devoted to the flesh and the world. Under that governance Adam, the first man, died, leaving to all posterity the testament of dying once. But the fourth mover or angel of Mercury, Raphael, influencing worldly things after Zachariel, began in the one thousand fifty-fifth year, at the end of the month of February, and lasted until the one thousand four hundred tenth year of the world. Under him the use of letters is first said to have been invented. The letters then were, as they report, very different from those which the world has today, devised according to the form and likeness of trees, plants, and animals; yet these afterwards, over time, were altered in many ways, and assumed an easier manner of being formed and a more cultivated ornament. For the fictions of the poets said that Mercury was the presiding power over all literature, promising that great hidden secrets of things lay concealed in fables. After this, when the human race had multiplied and been spread everywhere over the whole earth, the unity of letters did not long remain; but the separation of bodies and minds far from one another discovered diverse and varied modes of writing, about which a long narration would be required from us. Plato the Philosopher, in the Phaedrus, letters and the use of writing.

[he] relates that a certain philosopher, Theut by name, first discovered the art of writing, and at the same time the reckoning of weights and numbers and a certain game of dice, and taught Thamus, king of the Egyptians. But concerning the other ancient men who are said to have handed down special letters to almost individual nations and peoples, which remain in use among them down to the present day, it is not my purpose on this occasion to set down or describe the account. For all the more learned men among us know that Cadmus, son of Agenor, king of the Phoenicians, is said first to have brought sixteen letters into Greece: α. β. γ. δ. ε. ζ. ι. λ. μ. ν. ο. π. ϱ. σ. τ. ψ. To these Palamedes, at the time of the Trojan War, is said to have added four: ξ. θ. φ. χ. And Pythagoras afterwards added the letter θ, so that there should be twenty-one. χ. κ. ω. were subsequently discovered by others. Gordanis, bishop of the Goths, gave his people letters proper to them. When the unity of language had been confounded, the simplicity of characters too was variously altered in many ways. Hence it came about that, in the course of time, the use of letters arrogated to itself such licence that not only individual peoples, but also particular men, fashioning new characters for letters at their own discretion, prepared hiding-places for their mysteries. Yet every writing in an unusual character will not be free from the suspicion of those who see it. Notwithstanding this, many kings, tyrants, and princes of old devised for themselves a manner of writing set apart from common use and familiar to themselves, taking thought for the suspicion of others, provided only that what they wished to remain secret was not perceived. In imitation of these, I, [unclear], wishing to bring this work of Polygraphy, as far as possible, to a completed end, have resolved in this sixth book, which is the last, to call back from the underworld certain characters of the ancients which have now passed out of human use, lest they perish utterly. First, then, we shall set down the ancient manner of writing of the Northmen.

Concerning the alphabet and the remarkable manner of writing of the Northmen, at the time when they were laying waste Gaul by their incursion

All the letters of the Greeks and Palestinians are numerical, as was said before, while of the Latins, which we Germans also use, only seven are referred to numbers, namely c, d, i, l, m, v, and x. But the Northmen, after they had once come forth with the Asiatic Dacians from the Scandian islands, which are now called Gothic, wandered through Gaul for more than forty years and devastated it most grievously. In order to take counsel for their secret affairs, as Bede the English monk testifies, they discovered from the letters of the Greeks a new and beautiful manner of writing, as follows. For they adapted the numbers of the Greeks, comprised in ten letters among the twenty-four letters, to Latin characters, and prudently hid our letters beneath a foreign form: that is, in the manner in which we use numbers in place of letters, when, for example, for a we put 1, for b 2, for c 3, for d 4, and so on consecutively to the end of the alphabet. It is indeed a beautiful and quite safe invention, which neither a Greek nor a Latin will easily understand. For the whole alphabet is not found in it, but only nine letters, and one numerical sign, namely g, which among them signifies six and in this manner of writing denotes f, the sixth letter of the Latins. Moreover, yielding to our German language, in which we were born, we have finally added w, double v, as the twenty-fourth letter of our nation, which, according to the Greek number, we have formed thus: kΛ. But we shall set down this writing of the Northmen from the following order of Greek letters, in imitation of them.

By the aid of this alphabet the Northmen, whatever they wished among themselves. No Greek could understand this method of writing, since, even if all those characters are Greek, nevertheless, because they represent Latin letters according to numerical order, they cannot be read either by a Greek or by a Latin who has not first acquired knowledge of this device. This mode of writing can also be varied in many ways, when by [metathesis?] of the number the letters too are changed. This can also be done with Greek letters [alone?], at the wish and discretion of any industrious writer. Nor will the manner of forming these characters be very difficult, especially for one who has had some practice. The characters set forth above also suit the German language sufficiently well, since with them we can denote all things that occur to us, in whatever speech we are skilled. Whenever iota is placed by itself, so that it may be known to denote the letter l, the tenth of the alphabet, it is marked above thus: ī.

On the Alphabet and Method of Writing of the Ancient Franks

It is the opinion of very many that the Germans once had letters from the Greeks, and they firmly affirm that they also used the Greek language, especially in their sacred rites. For they say [unclear] great [unclear] between the Greek language and ours has utterly destroyed [unclear]. That most learned man, once my teacher, Johannes Camerarius Dalburgius, the most reverend bishop of the church of Worms, had collected several thousand Greek words which have the same meaning in both languages, Greek and German. And Caesar testifies in his Commentaries that the ancient Druids in Gaul, priests of the sacred rites, used the Greek language, especially in sacred matters. But when the Romans were laying waste the world, they at last violently imposed the use of their own letters, together with their dominion, upon many nations. Finally, the remnants of the Trojans, who were afterwards called Franks, in the four hundred and fortieth year of the incarnation, went out from the borders of the Scythians, King Marcomer providing leadership, came into Germany, and received settlements from their Saxon brothers at the mouths of the Rhine. Thereafter, for nine hundred and fifty years they waged an almost continual war with the Romans and the Gauls and, as Hunibald is the authority, finally brought almost all Europe under their empire or kingdom. Yet they did not abolish the letters of the Romans once they had received them, but rather, being themselves mingled among the Germans and Gauls, learned their language, and preserved their letters and the form of their writings. The writer of the histories of this people, Wasthald, wrote in his native tongue books of the deeds of kings, dukes, and princes over almost seven hundred and fifty-eight years, with the characters appended, as Hunibald says, which he mentions in his volume that he published in eighteen books on the origin of the Franks.

Unless a fault of the scribe has deceived me, I have represented Wasthald’s alphabet suitably, as I think; in it some characters differ altogether from the Greek, and some also seem partly to resemble them. Yet I do not know what to judge: whoever their inventor may have been, although he did not keep the form of the Greek letters, he observed the order of the letters. The codex, falling apart from excessive age, could scarcely be read; hence I fear that I have been deceived by some interpolator rather than found the true and certain opinion of Hunibald.

But let us pass on to what remains, since, if Hunibald’s statement is true, it will have been well written by us; but if it is the fiction of someone, it will neither harm us nor wrong the reader. There follows another fictitious alphabet found in the codex of Hunibald, to which this was inscribed:

The Alphabet of the Franks, Which Doracus Invented

Whoever wishes to use the characters set forth above should know that they are to be written beneath the lines, in the manner of the Greeks, not above as the Latins do. Likewise it must be observed that, of the double letters, the first are written at the beginning and in the middle of words, but the second always at the end.

From the Grammar of Otfrid, Monk of Weissenburg

Leginus [says] that Charles, king of the Franks, surnamed the Great, taking pity on the barbarism of his nation, attempted, with Nanno, Theobald, Albinus, and Berengar as helpers, to regulate the German language. And although, as Turpin testifies, he had begun so arduous a work, he did not complete it, being delayed by frequent incursions of wars, but, overtaken by death, left it unfinished; nor after him did another arise who would call back to mind the care of this matter. Otfrid

but the aforesaid monk, once a hearer and pupil of Rabanus of Fulda, under Louis the Pious, the son of Charles himself, having attained that grammar, though imperfectly, wrote many things in our German tongue, which seem to sound forth the wondrous gravity of regular instruction. For he composed several poems according to the same norm, in both heroic and elegiac meter; moreover he also composed some things in prose, to Louis, king of Germany, son of Louis the Pious and brother of the emperor Lothar; also to Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, to the monks of Saint Gall, and to others. Having obtained fragments of this grammar, I too have extracted the present characters of the alphabet from many, lest they perish entirely. It is clear, on Otfrid’s testimony, that Charles devised several alphabets of his own, which he might use securely in secret matters with individual prefects throughout his very wide kingdom. From these letters, with Otfrid supplying them, we commit a few here.

Zι ϒ Ρ 7 B Φ λ Ι O 6 V Κ μ Π R 2 X Π φ Λ Q 9 Y Σ π Ψ T Z Ψ m ψ U

Charles the great king, most Christian emperor, fought for thirty years with the Saxons, whom at last, overcoming them by the sword, he converted to the Christian faith. But fearing lest they should again, as they had done several times, apostatize from the faith, he established certain secret investigators, to whom he gave judicial power, who, traversing all Saxony, should secretly and diligently inquire into the faith and morals of the people; and whomever they found to have apostatized from the faith, or to be robbers, adulterers, blasphemers, contemners of the Church or of its priests and commandments, or disturbing the Christian commonwealth with notorious crimes, or recalling or soliciting the people to paganism, they should, without delay, by imperial and royal authority, with impunity hang by the noose, or kill by other means as they could. In order that this institution might remain forever unshaken, he gave these same men the power of substituting also other suitable men under fixed conditions, who, enjoying the aforesaid authority, should exercise with impunity the office of inquiry and of death upon the guilty. Finally he prescribed for them secret laws, hidden signs, and at the same time a form of oath, by which they might proceed justly in judging and punishing, and, being mutually known to one another, remain hidden from others, and perpetually preserve in the land of Saxony the necessary judgment in greater secrecy. They also used certain alphabets among themselves for a time, which, however, at length entirely fell out of use. Yet the office of this sort of inquiry remains down to the present time, whose ministers are commonly called Feimeri.

Although these characters do not appear sufficiently beautiful and elegant, nevertheless it has pleased me to join them with the foregoing new inventions of mine, for the honor and reverence of antiquity, since there is no one, even of little industry, who could not devise prettier ones for himself at his own discretion. Although continuous practice in writing will be able, by easy compensation, to amend this misshapen crookedness and, when often brought into habit, to make it pleasing. For no one, however learned or educated in any language, becomes a good writer unless by long practice in writing he has transformed usage into art. Another follows.

If anyone should wish to fashion for himself a new alphabet according to his own discretion, let him know that two things must especially be observed, which nevertheless I do not always find preserved in the preceding examples. The first is that he form characters of easy tracing, and the simpler they are, the better they will be. The second is that he order the individual letters in such a way that, joined into words, they present a beautiful and elegant appearance. I add a third, not promised: if you wish the writing to remain secret, make some letters of the alphabet double, in the manner of the Hebrews.

This Hichus, a Frank, together with Marcomer, restored [the people] from the borders of Scythia to the mouths of the Rhine into Germany; and for the supplement of the German language he is said to have invented these characters, which indeed seem to agree well enough with it in many respects.

Pharamund also, king of the Franks in Germany after Marcomer (who had led the people in)—the forty-third [king], and who died in the four hundred and twenty-sixth year of the Lord's nativity—when he had sent his scouts through Gaul for the sake of invading, ordered them to write in such characters:

[cipher/character table, as printed]

Besides that alphabet of the Normans which we set down at the beginning of this sixth book, we have also found the following one drawn up in Bede, which we commit to letters:

[alphabet table: A a B b C c … Z z]

From Latin letters, too, manifold alphabets are made—whether reduced to number according to the exemplar which we handed down in the preceding fifth book, or otherwise, in imitation of the Normans, with Greek letters also they afford our [men] a most safe means of announcing whatever we wish. Let us accordingly set down, according to the number and order of our usual alphabet, the letters themselves changed in an unusual way, and we shall have a secret and mystic mode of writing—fair and graceful enough, confirmed by usage. But this mode of numbering differs from that which we set down in the fifth book, and is more suited to our purpose.

[number-table: a=1, b=2, c=3 … t=20 … u=1900, v=28000, w=47000 … as printed]

With these principles of numbering by our letters rightly understood, [one will be able] now to carry the number out to any progression whatever, just as is sufficiently shown in the preceding book. Now let us arrange an alphabet from these.

[substitution alphabet table A–Z, as printed]

You now have, from Latin letters, a foreign alphabet, such as (we said above) the Normans once made for themselves from Greek; with which, the necessary diligence observed, you will write safely to a knowing friend whatever you wish for the time. Let us add another also, which we judge more secure.

[substitution/cipher table, as printed]

Although in Latin speech k, y, and w are not needful to us, yet because we use k and w in German, we have carried this alphabet too out to the twenty-fourth [letter], it also to be extended. And this mode of writing, too, can be variously multiplied at will. [cipher line, illegible] … according to the will of every writer.

There follows another alphabet of Honorius, surnamed the Theban, by whose ministry he hid his follies in magical [arts], as Peter of Abano testifies in his greater fourth book.

[Honorius cipher alphabet table, as printed]

I found also another alphabet, newly devised by a certain alchemist, which he was accustomed to use in concealing his secrets, making a great estimation of his art, which contains little in itself except words. For alchemy is loved by many, and is chaste.

[a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z]

Alchemy has many household attendants, who guard their mistress with perpetual vigilance, and put themselves forward under her name, so that they may preserve her, untouched for all time, from intercourse with so many importunate lovers. Vanity, fraud, deceitfulness, deception, sophistry, greed, falsehood, lying confidence, folly, want, poverty, despair, flight, proscription, and beggary are the maidservants of alchemy; pretending to love their mistress, they keep her inviolate, and very readily prostitute themselves to her moneyed, avaricious, greedy, and foolish seekers.

On the signs and wonderful, but excessively laborious, method of writing of M. T. Cicero, and after him of Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr

Marcus Tullius Cicero, the eloquent orator of the Romans, wrote a book of signs of no small size, which Saint Cyprian, bishop of the Carthaginians and martyr, enlarged with many signs and words, adding terms necessary for Christian usage, so that the work itself became useful not only to pagans, but much more also to the faithful.

The codex is rare, and was found by me only once, and bought at a low price. For when, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1496, I was examining many libraries out of love for books, I found the aforesaid codex in a certain monastery of our order, neglected because of its great age, cast aside under dust and despised. I asked the abbot, a doctor of law, how much he valued it at. He replied that he would prefer to it the little works of Saint Anselm, recently printed. I went to the booksellers, since the matter took place in a metropolitan city; I bought the requested little works of Anselm for a sixth part of a florin, handed them to the rejoicing abbot and monks, and rescued the codex, now brought nearly to destruction. For they had resolved, for love of the parchment, [unclear].

[unclear] I went up, and, having been admitted by Johannes Keifersberg, the distinguished preacher of the place, into the library of the greater church, I found an entire Psalter written out in these same signs of Tullius and Cyprian, and most handsomely written with golden chapter initials. But an inscription by someone ignorant of the mystery had been placed outside as follows: “Psalter in the Armenian language.” I called in a doctor, showed the falsity, and advised that it be rewritten: “Psalter written in Ciceronian signs.” Whether he did so or not, I am uncertain, since I did not afterward return to that library. So that you may see, reader, the form of Cicero’s notation, we have decided to set down a few signs below.

[table of signs unclear]

This method of writing requires a great memory, and the labor of reading is utterly immense, where each character signifies either a whole word, or a final syllable, or some part of speech suitable for the composition of the whole. Therefore, setting aside all the signs, let us draw an alphabet from a few.

[alphabet and sign tables unclear]

Many other new alphabets could also be formed from Cicero’s signs; we leave their extraction to the discretion of anyone who wishes to undertake it. For the book is abundant, and contains many signs notably differing from one another, all of which serve those who write.

[alphabet and sign tables unclear]

This was the alphabet of Iaimiel, great king of the Articians, surnamed Megalopius, a most wise man, which he used in secret matters; and it too can be changed in many ways. To it, out of love for the prince, we have added this alphabet of ours below, in which, once it is used more often over time, the scribe will become more fluent.

[alphabet and sign tables unclear]

How we may safely write any secrets whatsoever also by numbers and by many other various methods.

These things are childish, I admit, since anyone, according to his own capacity and judgment, can devise many more elegant alphabets than we have set down in the volume. Therefore we knowingly omit many things which, by a similar reckoning, we judge to be childish, commonplace, and of little use. We fear that one day we shall be ashamed to have applied our mind to these trifles, more useful matters having been set aside. But I pray that my readers will pardon me, since my own will indeed drew me back from these childish studies, not to call them at least in part vain; but the urging of certain friends compelled me to write these things, friends to whom I could not refuse this without injury to the bond of friendship contracted. Nevertheless, moved by their entreaty, I have also connected the following chapter with the preceding writings, and have put numbers in place of letters. For the ancients set down various and manifold modes of writing by means of numerical figures. Therefore, persuaded by the prayers of friends, at the end of this sixth book we have placed a few methods out of many, by which the way to knowledge of others lies open even to those who do not know them. For if anyone takes pleasure in knowing these things, he will easily be able, once these are known, to ascend to higher matters, and to vary the methods discovered in manifold alternation according to his own judgment. As a beginning for this matter we have placed a table under the orchema, which, when the reading is varied in the form of a cross, will contain within itself ninety-six alphabets.

Orchema

Numerical orchema in place of letters.

[table of letters and numbers]

Whoever rightly understands the table of the orchema will compose for himself from it as many alphabets as he wishes. For example, we have placed the letters of the Latins transversely, facing one another at the four corners, so that we might provide the leap of transposition without limit. Writers will need diligence, lest the multitude of numbers confuse memory or understanding.

We do not expand the orchemata, moved by a reasoned cause, because, since in its progression it strays rather far, the immense labor has frightened the mind. We have also deliberately passed over unity without assigning it a place, since we judge it rash to put it before our inventions in order. For from those things which we have now shown by way of example, anyone who is capable in understanding will easily attain greater things. All things serve secrets.

To each of the twelve divisions of the Zodiac we have assigned individual alphabets by numbers, so that the sign of Aries, in place of a, has the numerical cipher .a.; ♋, 7; ♉, 8; Cancer, 9; ♎, 10; ♏, 11; and so throughout the whole alphabet.

Trithemius's tabular ciphers — the alphabet-rotation expansion figures (tabula recta / auersa / aucta), bigram grids, and the numerical Orchema. The source facsimile is shown alongside and is authoritative for the cipher. Where the OCR preserved the rows they are transcribed as a table (illegible cells marked —, OCR noise left visible); where it linearised the paired plaintext/cipher columns into identical rows, the misleading grid is omitted in favour of the facsimile. These figures are worked examples, not a single mechanical grid.

We have also assigned single alphabets to the seven planets from the numbers remaining after the twelve signs. And note that when a letter is doubled in the text, its number is not written twice, but once, and it is marked with a dot above.

Sixth

We have brought the sixth and last book of our Polygraphy to its conclusion, by God’s mercy. In it, as we end our discourse with the wandering stars, we give the reader warning on certain points.

First, whenever he uses an alphabet, let him prudently add the character or mark of whatever sign or planet it is, for the sake of a double utility. For by this a great deal of labor is spared the friendly reader, and the mystery will remain secret, since anyone ignorant of the art will think that a table written with numbers and marked beforehand with the characters of signs or planets pertains to the science of astronomy, and will suspect that no mystery at all lies hidden. For this reason we have not taken the official matter for the letters from unity, but from a distance, lest we furnish anyone with a mark of suspicion. Prudence, nevertheless, must be used by writers, since a shrewd reader who is touched by suspicion of something hidden, if he detects the function of one number, will easily calculate the whole alphabet.

Second, remember, whoever you are who desire to be a skilled practitioner of this matter, that whenever in any word a letter is doubled, as very often happens, it is to be written only once and marked above with a point. For example, I wish to write from the alphabet of Aries “Ioannes,” not doubling the letter which is n, but I write thus: 14. 16. 7. 18. 10. 23. Or “abbas”: 6. 7. 6. 23. “Ioannes, abbas,” so that every mark of suspicion may be removed. In similar cases one must proceed with similar caution, because unless the practitioner is endowed with skill and knows how to discover greater things from small ones, he will not be fit for these least matters of ours to be disclosed to him. Not all things are to be communicated everywhere to everyone, especially those whose use is capable of being turned to good and to evil.

Moved with reason by that consideration, we have plainly handed down many things in these six books of the Polygraphy for those who wish to know, but we have allowed far more secret things to lie hidden beneath what is plain. Finally, we have written a key that lays open the whole work, explaining how it is to be understood in each metaphor; yet by the advice of certain persons we have ordered it to remain hidden at home, so that students may not lack material for exercising the memory, and that the cause of knowing it may be taken away from the wicked, who are not willing to use it well. In every passage many mysteries lie hidden, and the greater things you discover from them, the greater remain to be discovered.

A way is prepared for beginners; for those setting out upon it, it will not be difficult in the course of time to discover many things, both [unclear] and very great. Here one who did not know will learn to write Latin, and prudently to wrap all the mysteries of his will in foreign speech. But that the unlearned man may be able to understand not only his own mysteries which he wraps up, but also open speech of which until now he has always been ignorant, is not a task of great labor, if the interpreter has fully grasped our intention in this volume. For beneath the bark lie the kernels of our Steganography, buried for a just reason, lest they lie open to unworthy babblers. It was worth the labor, finally, that one work should not prejudice another, but that its own right should be distributed to each unimpaired.

Wearied after a long voyage, we here cast anchor in the sea, under the name of JESUS CHRIST, the Savior of the faithful, on the twenty-first day of the month of March, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1508, in the eleventh indiction of the Romans, at Würzburg, a city of the eastern Franks, which they call both Würzburg and Herbipolis.

End of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, abbot at Saint James in Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict

Correction.

The fair reader must be warned that the order of the books of this Polygraphy is especially to be observed, lest the division of the signature which occurred in the first alphabet perhaps give rise to error. For there the Key of the Polygraphy ends at c; after the remaining books, however, the fifth book begins again at d.

At Frankfurt, from the workshop of Cyriacus Jacobus.

In the year 1550.

2026-06-10 — crypto-cluster prose re-translation (Fable 5, facsimile pass)

full_chunk_0033

Re-translated from scratch against the source page-scans, superseding the earlier machine rendering, and independently re-graded against the Latin; the superseded text is retained in version control.

What was wrong: The prior public rendering ended with a genuinely truncated, opaque clause ("'When she asks for papers to be hidden, tied to the leg,' and [unclear]") that misrepresented the segment boundary, and it silently normalized a print misprint without recording the crux. The segment is ordinary continuous prose: a chain of steganography anecdotes from Pliny (tithymalus/invisible milk-writing), Theodorus Bibliander's hyphasmaticon/hyphalmicon note, Herodotus on Demaratus' wax tablets and Gorgo's interpretation, Gellius 17.9 on Histiaeus' tattooed slave, Herodotus 1.123 on Harpagus' gutted hare to Cyrus (cf. Justin 1), the Mutina carrier-pigeons (Hirtius/Decimus Brutus), and secret inks, closing on an Ovid quotation. None of the prose was fabricated, but the ending and several proper names needed repair against the scans.

Key corrections (verified against the scan): - Recovered the truncated ending from the scans: the segment closes mid-couplet on the hexameter only, 'Cum poscit cruri chartas celare ligatas,' = Ovid, Ars Amatoria 3.621; rendered it faithfully and reserved [unclear] for the deliberate mid-couplet cut (the pentameter 'Et iuncto blandas sub pede ferre notas' is the catchword 'Et iun-' on p.68 and belongs to segment 34), instead of the prior vague paraphrase 'papers to be hidden, tied to the leg'. - Flagged the print crux at the Gorgo passage: the 1518 print itself reads 'Chromenis filia' (so the OCR is a faithful witness), a typographical error for 'Cleomenis'; restored the historically correct 'Gorgo, daughter of Cleomenes and wife of Leonidas' and recorded the misprint in the note (prior text emended silently). - Verified and restored proper names against the print: Theodorus Bibliander, Demaratus, Susa, Xerxes, Histiaeus, Darius, Aristagoras, Astyages, Harpagus, Cyrus, Tithymalus; and noted that the print's 'Hyrcius'/'Decius Brutus' (siege of Mutina) are Hirtius and Decimus Brutus. - Italicized the two run-in lemma headings per house style: 'The second kind: hyphasmaticon.' and 'Letters are likewise written in various other ways.'; tightened the Harpagus/Cyrus and Histiaeus passages for fidelity (e.g., 'tattooed the smooth head with the forms of letters', 'most trusted household huntsmen').

Surviving cruxes: - Print reads 'Chromenis filia' — a 1518 misprint for 'Cleomenis' (Cleomenes); historical name restored, misprint noted. - Segment 33 deliberately ends mid-couplet after the Ovid hexameter (Ars Am. 3.621); [unclear] marks the intentional cut at catchword 'Et iun-', not illegible print — the pentameter continues in segment 34. - Print's 'Hyrcius' and 'Decius Brutus' = Aulus Hirtius and Decimus Brutus; restored with print forms noted. - Pliny citation printed as 'lib. 26' for the tithymalus/invisible-writing detail; rendered as 'book 26' following the print.
